body:
India's institutions and their different responsibilities

India's space and defence-electronics capabilities involve several organisations with distinct roles. ISRO, the Indian Space Research Organisation, develops space systems and applications, including satellites for communication, navigation and Earth observation. DRDO, the Defence Research and Development Organisation, develops a wide range of defence technologies, including electronic-warfare systems and associated capabilities.

An ISRO satellite and a DRDO defence system may support related national requirements, but the organisations and their projects should not be treated as identical.

India's communication and observation satellite programmes

INSAT and IRS

The Indian National Satellite System (INSAT) became established in 1983 with INSAT-1B. It developed into an important system for telecommunications, broadcasting, weather-related services and other applications.

The Indian Remote Sensing (IRS) programme is associated with collecting observations of Earth. IRS-1A was launched in March 1988. Remote sensing provides information about the Earth's surface, whereas communication satellites principally transfer information between users.

The two names describe different major applications. They are not exhaustive classifications of every modern Indian satellite.

GSAT-7 and GSAT-7A

GSAT-7 was launched on 30 August 2013. It is a communication satellite designed to serve users over the Indian landmass and a wide oceanic region. Its application concerns communication rather than direct optical reconnaissance.

GSAT-7A was launched on 19 December 2018 by GSLV-F11. It is also a communication satellite, designed to provide services over the Indian region.

EMISAT

EMISAT was launched on 1 April 2019 by PSLV-C45. ISRO states that it was placed into a 748 km sun-synchronous polar orbit and was intended for electromagnetic-spectrum measurement.

EMISAT is useful for understanding the relationship between electronic sensing and space systems. Its officially stated electromagnetic-measurement purpose should not be confused with an ordinary communication-relay role.

EOS-04

EOS-04 was launched on 14 February 2022 by PSLV-C52 into a sun-synchronous polar orbit of approximately 529 km. It is a radar-imaging satellite designed to obtain Earth-observation data under a wide range of weather conditions.

ISRO identifies agriculture, forestry, soil moisture, hydrology and flood mapping among its applications. The mission demonstrates the usefulness of radar imaging; it should not automatically be described as a dedicated military surveillance satellite.

GSAT-7R, also called CMS-03

GSAT-7R (CMS-03) was launched on 2 November 2025 by LVM3-M5. It is a communication satellite associated with the Indian Navy and intended to strengthen maritime communications across the Indian Ocean Region.

Its role includes supporting communication links among naval users. The spacecraft should not be confused with a navigation satellite or an anti-satellite weapon.

NavIC: India's regional navigation system

Navigation with Indian Constellation (NavIC), formerly known as the Indian Regional Navigation Satellite System (IRNSS), is India's indigenous regional satellite-navigation system. It is designed to provide positioning, navigation and timing services.

NavIC's primary service area covers India and approximately 1,500 km beyond the Indian boundary. The original constellation design includes 7 satellites:

  • 3 geostationary satellites, which appear fixed relative to Earth.
  • 4 inclined geosynchronous satellites, which have a geosynchronous period but do not appear fixed at one point.

NavIC provides two principal categories of navigation service:

  • Standard Positioning Service (SPS): Intended for civilian users.
  • Restricted Service (RS): An encrypted service intended for authorised users, including strategic users.

NavIC is a regional navigation system, not a system designed to provide the same primary coverage worldwide as GPS. Its services are concerned with position and time. They are not equivalent to satellite photographs or ordinary two-way voice communication.

Launch and operational status are different facts

ISRO's 25 February 2026 report on NVS-02 stated that the spacecraft had been launched into an elliptical transfer orbit on 29 January 2025, but the planned orbit-raising operations could not be completed. In ISRO's Spacecraft Missions status list, consulted on 14 November 2026, NVS-02 was listed as not operational.

This is a status statement about NVS-02, not a claim that the entire NavIC system is non-operational. The same ISRO status list identified NVS-01 as operational for positioning, navigation and timing service.

Gujarat's contribution: Space Applications Centre, Ahmedabad

The Space Applications Centre (SAC) is an ISRO centre located in Ahmedabad, Gujarat. It was established in 1972 through the integration of space-application activities in Ahmedabad.

SAC develops space-borne and airborne instruments, satellite payloads and applications associated with communication, navigation and remote sensing. Its work includes communication transponders for Indian satellite programmes.

This is a genuine Gujarat connection to strategic and civilian space technology: equipment developed in Ahmedabad contributes to national satellite capabilities that serve applications far beyond Gujarat.

Remember the major mission milestones

Prelims focus

  • INSAT was established in 1983; IRS-1A was launched in March 1988.
  • GSAT-7: 30 August 2013; GSAT-7A: 19 December 2018. Both are communication satellites.
  • EMISAT: 1 April 2019, PSLV-C45, electromagnetic-spectrum measurement, 748 km sun-synchronous polar orbit.
  • EOS-04: 14 February 2022, radar imaging; GSAT-7R (CMS-03): 2 November 2025, naval communication.
  • NavIC: regional navigation, 7-satellite original design, India plus approximately 1,500 km, SPS and RS.
  • Trap: SAC is an ISRO centre in Ahmedabad, not a DRDO electronic-warfare laboratory.

[Sources: NCERT, India: People and Economy, Class 12, Chapter 10, Transport and Communication, printed p. 123; ISRO, Communication Satellites, INSAT section, consulted 14 November 2026; ISRO, GSAT-7, GSAT-7A, EMISAT, PSLV-C52/EOS-04 Mission and Satellite Navigation Services, respective Mission and Programme sections, consulted 14 November 2026; Ministry of Defence, Press Information Bureau, Indian Navy to Bolster Space-Based Communication with Indigenous GSAT-7R Satellite, 2 November 2025; ISRO, Spacecraft Missions, status list consulted 14 November 2026; ISRO, NVS-02 Spacecraft: On-Orbit Observations and Apex Committee Recommendations, 25 February 2026; ISRO, Space Applications Centre, About section, consulted 14 November 2026; Department of Space, Rajya Sabha Reply on Space Applications Centre in ISRO, 4 August 2022.]

body:
Why space systems can become strategic targets

Satellites support communication, navigation, surveillance, weather services and other activities. When a military organisation depends on these services, the loss or degradation of a space system can affect operations on Earth.

A satellite system includes more than a spacecraft. It also depends on ground control, communication links, data processing and user equipment. Consequently, disruption may affect the satellite itself, its signals, the ground segment or the service received by users.

Understanding anti-satellite activity

Anti-satellite (ASAT) capability refers to the ability to attack, disable, damage or otherwise interfere with satellites or their functions. Different forms of interference or attack can produce different effects.

At the introductory level, a useful distinction is between physical destruction and disruption of a satellite-dependent service.

  • Kinetic anti-satellite action: A physical impact damages or destroys a satellite. Such an event may create orbital debris.
  • Electronic interference: An electromagnetic link used by a satellite-dependent service is degraded or disrupted. The satellite itself may remain physically intact.
  • Cyber compromise: Computers, software or digital information associated with a space service are improperly accessed, altered or disrupted.

These categories are useful for distinguishing mechanisms, but the terms should not be treated as proof that every service outage was caused by an attack. Natural events, equipment failure and operational errors can also disrupt space services.

Mission Shakti: India's anti-satellite test

On 27 March 2019, the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) conducted Mission Shakti, an anti-satellite missile test. The test took place from Dr A. P. J. Abdul Kalam Island in Odisha.

According to the Ministry of Defence, a DRDO-developed interceptor successfully struck an Indian target satellite in low Earth orbit in a physical hit-to-kill engagement.

Mission Shakti demonstrated a kinetic anti-satellite capability. It was not a test of NavIC's positioning accuracy, a communication satellite launch or an example of electronic jamming.

Mission Shakti: 27 March 2019, DRDO, Indian satellite target, low Earth orbit, kinetic anti-satellite test.

Space debris and collision hazards

Space debris includes non-functional satellites, discarded rocket components and fragments created through accidents, break-ups or destructive events. Debris can remain in orbit and may threaten operational spacecraft.

Even relatively small fragments can be dangerous because orbital objects can move at very high relative speeds. A destructive anti-satellite event may therefore create risks beyond the immediate loss of the target satellite.

Debris hazards explain an important difference between a temporary loss of signal and the physical destruction of a spacecraft. Interference may stop when the cause is removed; fragments produced by a destructive event may remain a problem for other space objects.

Space situational awareness

Space situational awareness (SSA) is knowledge of objects, activities and conditions in the space environment that helps identify potential risks to space operations.

SSA includes monitoring operational satellites, non-functional objects and debris; estimating their orbits; and assessing whether objects may approach one another dangerously.

When a collision risk is identified, an operational satellite may be able to perform a collision-avoidance manoeuvre, subject to its available capability and the assessed circumstances. Another important measure is the responsible management of spacecraft at the end of their missions.

India's ISRO System for Safe and Sustainable Space Operations Management (IS4OM) supports these activities. It is concerned with monitoring space objects, assessing collision risks and helping protect Indian space assets.

SSA is not the same as reconnaissance of Earth's surface. Earth-observation reconnaissance looks towards terrestrial features and activities. Space situational awareness focuses on objects and hazards associated with the space environment.

Resilience: maintaining essential services

Resilience is the ability of a system to withstand disruption, continue essential functions where possible and recover after an interruption. A resilient defence system does not depend entirely on one satellite, one ground station or one communication path.

Several broad principles help explain resilience:

  • Redundancy: More than one suitable component or service may be available for an essential function.
  • Diverse communication paths: Satellite and terrestrial links may complement one another where available.
  • Protected digital systems: Authentication, access controls and integrity safeguards help prevent unauthorised manipulation of information.
  • Space-object monitoring: SSA provides information useful for reducing collision risks.
  • Recovery arrangements: Organisations prepare to restore essential functions after a component or service becomes unavailable.

Redundancy does not eliminate every risk. Several systems can still fail because of a shared dependency, a widespread disturbance or insufficient alternative coverage. The central principle is to avoid unnecessary dependence on a single vulnerable point.

India's defence-space coordination

India's Defence Space Agency (DSA) supports coordination concerning military use and protection of space capabilities. It is distinct from the Defence Cyber Agency, whose focus is cyber threats and capabilities.

The Defence Space Agency conducted Antariksha Abhyas 2024, a space-focused exercise held from 11 to 13 November 2024. The Ministry of Defence described its focus as improving understanding of threats to space-based assets and services and strengthening coordination among the armed forces.

The exercise was an activity concerned with preparedness and coordination. It should not be confused with the 2019 Mission Shakti anti-satellite test.

Connecting the whole subtopic

Electronic warfare, cyber warfare and space systems are closely related because satellites and defence networks depend on both electromagnetic signals and digital information. However, their concepts remain distinct.

Electronic support observes emissions. Electronic attack disrupts or misleads electromagnetic systems. Electronic protection helps friendly electronic systems remain usable. Cybersecurity protects digital systems and information. Space reconnaissance collects observations, navigation provides position and time, and space situational awareness helps protect spacecraft against hazards.

Prelims focus

  • Mission Shakti was conducted by DRDO on 27 March 2019 against an Indian satellite in LEO.
  • Mission Shakti was a kinetic anti-satellite test, not an electronic-jamming operation.
  • Space debris includes fragments from destructive events and can threaten operational satellites.
  • IS4OM is associated with ISRO and space situational awareness.
  • Antariksha Abhyas 2024 was conducted by the Defence Space Agency from 11 to 13 November 2024.
  • Trap: Disruption of a satellite service does not necessarily mean the satellite has been physically destroyed.

[Sources: Ministry of Defence, Press Information Bureau, India Joins Select Group of Nations, Destroys Live Satellite in Low Earth Orbit, 27 March 2019; ISRO, Dedication of ISRO System for Safe and Sustainable Operations Management (IS4OM) to the Nation, programme description, consulted 14 November 2026; ISRO, Space Situational Assessment 2021, Space Debris and Space Situational Awareness sections; ISRO, Indian Space Situational Awareness Report for 2025, released 16 April 2026, Background section; Ministry of Defence, Press Information Bureau, Defence Space Agency Successfully Conducts Maiden Exercise Antariksha Abhyas 2024, 13 November 2024; DRDO/DESIDOC, Electronic Warfare, 1988, Chapter 2, Electronic Warfare Definitions.]
